current downstream plugin-packaging boundary and validator expectations\\\\n\\\\n### Institutional Learnings\\\\n\\\\n- Keep local packaging canonical while importing useful upstream improvements; do not let the Anthropic reference reopen local family-boundary churn.\\\\n- This repo works best when the contract is visible in both markdown and the validator or report outputs that maintainers actually use.\\\\n- For repo-focused closeout, the standard broad validation path remains preflight first and `bash Infrastructure/scripts/validation-and-linting/verify-work.sh` before completion claims.\\\\n\\\\n### External References\\\\n\\\\n- Anthropic pinned `skill-creator` at commit `98669c11ca63e9c81c11501e1437e5c47b556621`\\\\n- OpenAI and Codex guidance already incorporated into the governing spec as of 2026-04-04\\\\n\\\\n## Key Technical Decisions\\\\n\\\\n- Decision 1: Use a dedicated target-skill artifact file at `Infrastructure/references/handoff-package.md` as the phase-one `HandoffPackage` path.\\\\n  - Rationale: it is durable, repo-visible, naturally colocated with the authored skill, and distinct from chat-only summaries or repo-global plan docs.\\\\n\\\\n- Decision 2: Reuse existing machine-readable eval outputs and add only one small human-review surface when necessary.\\\\n  - Rationale: `result.json`, `summary.json`, `scorecard.json`, and `release_manifest.json` already exist. The lowest-churn upgrade is to enrich them with round-state and baseline metadata, and add `comparison_review.md` only for the qualitative side the current artifacts do not express clearly enough.\\\\n  - Phase-one ownership map:\\\\n    - `result.json`: per-case candidate-versus-baseline evidence, round state, metric availability state, and optional qualitative-review artifact pointer\\\\n    - `summary.json`: run-level rollup of readiness decisions, blocked rounds, and neutral-baseline justification references\\\\n    - `scorecard.json`: CI-facing normalized pass/fail surface that stays additive and does not become the canonical narrative record\\\\n    - `release_manifest.json`: thin release-facing snapshot that references richer report artifacts rather than duplicating every round-detail field\\\\n    - `comparison_review.md`: optional run-scoped human-readable comparison artifact under the reports directory, not a versioned skill artifact\\\\n\\\\n- Decision 3: Keep `neutral_repo_baseline` planner-approved and human-justified only.\\\\n  - Rationale: allowing the builder lane to improvise baselines would weaken the whole comparative loop.\\\\n  - Phase-one source of truth: store the human approval and justification in `Skills/skill-builder/Infrastructure/references/evals.yaml`, and require run artifacts to copy or reference that record rather than inventing a parallel approval surface.\\\\n\\\\n- Decision 4: Require route and description assessment in every non-trivial round, but require edits only when the evidence shows weakness or ambiguity.\\\\n  - Rationale: this keeps the loop disciplined without forcing meaningless churn into every pass.\\\\n\\\\n- Decision 5: Treat skill-sync and catalog regeneration as part of closeout when user-facing skill descriptions or metadata change.\\\\n  - Rationale: the family is public-facing, and stale indexes would make the new contract partially invisible even if the files themselves are correct.\\\\n\\\\n## Open Questions\\\\n\\\\n### Resolved During Planning\\\\n\\\\n- What should the smallest durable creator-to-builder artifact be?\\\\n  - Resolution: `Infrastructure/references/handoff-package.md` inside the target skill.\\\\n\\\\n- Which repo-native artifact should carry comparative review evidence?\\\\n  - Resolution: enrich the existing JSON report surfaces first; add `comparison_review.md` per run only for the human-readable qualitative delta that current JSON artifacts do not already express.\\\\n\\\\n- Should route and description optimization be mandatory every round?\\\\n  - Resolution: assessment is mandatory every non-trivial round; edits are mandatory only when evidence shows trigger weakness, ambiguity, or misleading descriptions.\\\\n\\\\n### Deferred to Implementation\\\\n\\\\n- Whether `Skills/skill-creator/Infrastructure/scripts/init_skill.py` should auto-scaffold a starter `Infrastructure/references/handoff-package.md` placeholder, or whether a reference template plus `SKILL.md` guidance is sufficient for phase one.\\\\n  - Deferred because the lower-churn path should be chosen after the execution pass confirms whether deterministic scaffolding materially reduces drift.\\\\n  - Phase-one decision rule: keep this docs-and-template only unless execution shows repeated artifact omission, validator ambiguity, or enough repeated manual drift that the template is no longer a reliable contract.\\\\n\\\\n- Whether `release_manifest.json` should duplicate all new readiness-state fields, or only reference the richer `summary.json` and per-case `result.json` outputs.\\\\n  - Deferred because the existing consumers may only need a narrow additive change.\\\\n  - Phase-one decision rule: keep `release_manifest.json` thin by default and only duplicate new readiness fields when a real consumer proves the pointer-plus-summary model is insufficient.\\\\n\\\\n## References](#sources-and-references)\\\\n\\\\n## Enhancement Summary\\\\n\\\\n**Deepened on:** 2026-04-04  \\\\n**Mode:** targeted-confidence  \\\\n**Key areas improved:** artifact ownership, unit sequencing, blocker classification, and closeout verification\\\\n\\\\n- Added an explicit artifact-ownership matrix so `ce-work` can land the builder and harness changes without re-deciding where round metadata belongs.\\\\n- Tightened the deferred implementation questions with phase-one decision rules instead of leaving both as open-ended execution judgment.\\\\n- Strengthened validation and blocker-control gates so compatibility regressions, runner noise, and partial-rollout drift are classified consistently before closeout.\\\\n\\\\n## Overview\\\\n\\\\nUpgrade the skill-authoring family from a clean routing split into a coherent, evidence-backed authoring loop without undoing the lifecycle boundaries that were just stabilized.\\\\n\\\\nThis plan implements the approved spec by:\\\\n- making `skill-creator` produce a durable creator-to-builder handoff artifact for non-trivial skills;\\\\n- teaching `skill-builder` one explicit comparative iteration loop with frozen inputs, baseline rules, round states, and visible review evidence;\\\\n- keeping `skill-installer` and `plugin-builder` as downstream-only owners gated by `ContractValidityEvidence`;\\\\n- extending existing repo-native eval and reporting surfaces instead of introducing a new standalone viewer or parallel harness.\\\\n\\\\nPlan mode: `standard-plan`  \\\\nPlan depth: `deep`  \\\\nExecution posture: artifact-contract-first, then builder evidence surfaces, then eval enforcement, then downstream gating and full-family validation.\\\\n\\\\n## Problem Frame\\\\n\\\\nThe family routing contract is now clear, but the authoring loop still relies too much on implied escalation and loosely bundled evidence:\\\\n- `skill-creator` stops at starter drafting plus `quick_validate.py`, but does not yet leave behind one canonical durable artifact for the next stage;\\\\n- `skill-builder` already owns eval and description-optimization surfaces, but it does not yet present one first-class round model that explains how candidate and baseline runs are prepared, compared, reviewed, and promoted;\\\\n- downstream surfaces already point back to `skill-builder`, but they do not yet depend on one explicit evidence bundle and readiness-state story;\\\\n- existing report artifacts such as `result.json`, `summary.json`, `scorecard.json`, and `release_manifest.json` are useful, but they do not yet expose the specific comparative loop concepts the spec now requires.\\\\n\\\\nWithout a deliberate implementation sequence, execution will drift in one of two ways:\\\\n- the docs will describe the right lifecycle, but helper outputs and eval artifacts will still not prove it; or\\\\n- the harness will grow new fields and files ad hoc, but the family skills will still not teach the same contract to users and maintainers.\\\\n\\\\n## Requirements Trace\\\\n\\\\n- R1. Preserve the current family split and routing ownership across `skill-creator`, `skill-builder`, `skill-installer`, and `plugin-builder`.\\\\n  Trace: spec goals 1 and 7; `SA1`\\\\n- R2. Non-trivial creator-stage work must end with a durable dedicated handoff artifact file carrying the required context fields.\\\\n  Trace: spec `HandoffPackage`; spec invariants; `SA2`, `SA2a`, `SA3`\\\\n- R3. `skill-builder` must expose one explicit non-trivial iteration loop with prompt preparation, baseline selection, frozen comparison inputs, evidence capture, tuning assessment, and round decision.\\\\n  Trace: spec `IterationRound`, `ComparisonInputs`, `IterationRoundState`; `SA4`, `SA5`, `SA7`, `SA14`, `SA15`\\\\n- R4. Comparative evidence must preserve both machine-readable and human-reviewable signals, including metric unavailability and readiness-state distinctions.\\\\n  Trace: spec `EvalEvidenceBundle`; failure model; observability; `SA6`, `SA17`\\\\n- R5. Install and plugin packaging surfaces must remain downstream-only and require `ContractValidityEvidence`.\\\\n  Trace: spec downstream handoff rules; `SA9`, `SA10`, `SA18`\\\\n- R6. The implementation must stay repo-native by extending existing docs, eval manifests, and report artifacts instead of introducing a new viewer or cloned upstream workspace.\\\\n  Trace: spec goals 8 and non-goals; `SA11`, `SA12`, `SA13`\\\\n\\\\n## Scope Boundaries\\\\n\\\\nIn scope:\\\\n- authoring-family skill docs and metadata:\\\\n  - `Skills/skill-creator/`\\\\n  - `Skills/skill-builder/`\\\\n  - `Skills/skill-installer/`\\\\n  - `Skills/plugin-builder/`\\\\n- creator-stage artifact guidance and reusable template support\\\\n- `skill-builder` iteration, evidence, and reporting contract\\\\n- eval harness additions required to protect the new loop\\\\n- downstream handoff wording and readiness gating\\\\n- repo validation and sync work needed to keep public skill surfaces aligned\\\\n\\\\nOut of scope:\\\\n- merging or renaming the family\\\\n- a repo-wide skill-evals platform redesign\\\\n- a new dedicated UI artifact or UI plan\\\\n- a new standalone viewer application for eval review\\\\n- policy changes that would make `skill-builder` explicit-only\\\\n- runtime router changes outside the named family surfaces and existing eval/reporting helpers\\\\n\\\\n## Context and Research\\\\n\\\\n### Relevant Code and Patterns\\\\n\\\\n- `Docs/specs/2026-04-03-feat-skill-authoring-family-contract-spec.md`\\\\n  - authoritative contract for the creator handoff, builder round model, baseline rules, observability, and downstream gating\\\\n- `docs/brainstorms/2026-04-03-skill-authoring-family-contract-requirements.md`\\\\n  - existing deterministic scaffolding surface if template emission or signposting needs automation\\\\n- `Skills/skill-builder/SKILL.md`\\\\n  - current lifecycle-maintenance contract with smoke/release eval and description-optimization references\\\\n- `Skills/skill-builder/Infrastructure/references/iteration-and-testing.md`\\\\n  - likely home for the explicit round model if `SKILL.md` needs slimmer routing-level guidance\\\\n- `Skills/skill-builder/Infrastructure/references/description-optimization.md`\\\\n  - existing route/description improvement guidance that can become one named step in the new round\\\\n- `Skills/skill-builder/Infrastructure/references/evals.yaml`\\\\n  - current regression suite already covering routing and packaging boundaries\\\\n- `Skills/skill-builder/Infrastructure/scripts/run_skill_evals.py`\\\\n  - current machine-readable report surface writing `result.json`, `summary.json`, `scorecard.json`, `release_manifest.json`, and `junit.xml`\\\\n- `Skills/skill-builder/Infrastructure/scripts/test_run_skill_evals.py`\\\\n  - existing regression suite for eval-mode and runner-shape behavior\\\\n- `Skills/skill-builder/Infrastructure/references/release-manifest.template.json`\\\\n  - current artifact contract template for release runs\\\\n- `Skills/skill-builder/Infrastructure/references/quality-tools.md`\\\\n  - canonical docs for report outputs and validator expectations\\\\n- `Skills/skill-installer/SKILL.md`\\\\n  - current downstream install/import boundary and provenance language\\\\n- `Skills/plugin-builder/SKILL.md`\\\\n  - Rationale: it is durable, repo-visible, naturally colocated with the authored skill, and distinct from chat-only summaries or repo-global plan docs.\\\\n\\\\n- Decision 2: Reuse existing machine-readable eval outputs and add only one small human-review surface when necessary.\\\\n  - Rationale: `result.json`, `summary.json`, `scorecard.json`, and `release_manifest.json` already exist. The lowest-churn upgrade is to enrich them with round-state and baseline metadata, and add `comparison_review.md` only for the qualitative side the current artifacts do not express clearly enough.\\\\n  - Phase-one ownership map:\\\\n    - `result.json`: per-case candidate-versus-baseline evidence, round state, metric availability state, and optional qualitative-review artifact pointer\\\\n    - `summary.json`: run-level rollup of readiness decisions, blocked rounds, and neutral-baseline justification references\\\\n    - `scorecard.json`: CI-facing normalized pass/fail surface that stays additive and does not become the canonical narrative record\\\\n    - `release_manifest.json`: thin release-facing snapshot that references richer report artifacts rather than duplicating every round-detail field\\\\n    - `comparison_review.md`: optional run-scoped human-readable comparison artifact under the reports directory, not a versioned skill artifact\\\\n\\\\n- Decision 3: Keep `neutral_repo_baseline` planner-approved and human-justified only.\\\\n  - Rationale: allowing the builder lane to improvise baselines would weaken the whole comparative loop.\\\\n  - Phase-one source of truth: store the human approval and justification in `Skills/skill-builder/Infrastructure/references/evals.yaml`, and require run artifacts to copy or reference that record rather than inventing a parallel approval surface.\\\\n\\\\n- Decision 4: Require route and description assessment in every non-trivial round, but require edits only when the evidence shows weakness or ambiguity.\\\\n  - Rationale: this keeps the loop disciplined without forcing meaningless churn into every pass.\\\\n\\\\n- Decision 5: Treat skill-sync and catalog regeneration as part of closeout when user-facing skill descriptions or metadata change.\\\\n  - Rationale: the family is public-facing, and stale indexes would make the new contract partially invisible even if the files themselves are correct.\\\\n\\\\n## Open Questions\\\\n\\\\n### Resolved During Planning\\\\n\\\\n- What should the smallest durable creator-to-builder artifact be?\\\\n  - Resolution: `Infrastructure/references/handoff-package.md` inside the target skill.\\\\n\\\\n- Which repo-native artifact should carry comparative review evidence?\\\\n  - Resolution: enrich the existing JSON report surfaces first; add `comparison_review.md` per run only for the human-readable qualitative delta that current JSON artifacts do not already express.\\\\n\\\\n- Should route and description optimization be mandatory every round?\\\\n  - Resolution: assessment is mandatory every non-trivial round; edits are mandatory only when evidence shows trigger weakness, ambiguity, or misleading descriptions.\\\\n\\\\n### Deferred to Implementation\\\\n\\\\n- Whether `Skills/skill-creator/Infrastructure/scripts/init_skill.py` should auto-scaffold a starter `Infrastructure/references/handoff-package.md` placeholder, or whether a reference template plus `SKILL.md` guidance is sufficient for phase one.\\\\n  - Deferred because the lower-churn path should be chosen after the execution pass confirms whether deterministic scaffolding materially reduces drift.\\\\n  - Phase-one decision rule: keep this docs-and-template only unless execution shows repeated artifact omission, validator ambiguity, or enough repeated manual drift that the template is no longer a reliable contract.\\\\n\\\\n- Whether `release_manifest.json` should duplicate all new readiness-state fields, or only reference the richer `summary.json` and per-case `result.json` outputs.\\\\n  - Deferred because the existing consumers may only need a narrow additive change.\\\\n  - Phase-one decision rule: keep `release_manifest.json` thin by default and only duplicate new readiness fields when a real consumer proves the pointer-plus-summary model is insufficient.\\\\n\\\\n## High-Level Technical Design\\\\n\\\\n> This is directional planning guidance, not implementation code.\\\\n\\\\n```mermaid\\\\nflowchart LR\\\\n  A[\\\\\\\"skill-creator starter authoring\\\\\\\"] --> B[\\\\\\\"target skill Infrastructure/references/handoff-package.md\\\\\\\"]\\\\n  B --> C[\\\\\\\"skill-builder round preparation\\\\\\\"]\\\\n  C --> D[\\\\\\\"candidate and baseline notes:\\\\n- The creator-stage durable artifact should live with the target skill, not with the authoring-family skill itself.\\\\n- The builder loop should prefer additive artifact enrichment over a **Objective:** Ensure every run is resumable, safely abortable, and auditable with deterministic completion semantics.\\\\n- **Constraints:** No silent failures, no hidden side effects, and operator control must always outrank normal loop progress.\\\\n- **Failure cost if wrong:** accidental duplicate promotions, incomplete audit trail, and unauthorized canonical graph mutation.\\\\n\\\\n#### Parity and control map (high priority paths)\\\\n| User action | Agent capability path | Current gap |\\\\n|---|---|---|\\\\n| Trigger loop run | `recursive_skill_loop.py` CLI options + run directory contracts | Partial: kill/abort behavior is currently secondary to normal terminal transitions |\\\\n| Resume/replay after interruption | run-id + resume path + deterministic journals | Partial: stale/replay duplicate handling exists but needs explicit blocked + rollback state |\\\\n| Emergency stop run | No explicit kill-switch contract | **Gap (high):** no authoritative kill behavior for incident control |\\\\n| Approve canonical lesson | `human_promote_recursive_run.sh` + validator | Needs explicit version-locked rollback semantics |\\\\n| Roll back/undo bad run mutation | Not explicitly modeled | **Gap (high):** need terminal rollback and artifact cleanup contract |\\\\n\\\\n#### Execution-loop contract additions\\\\n- **Start:** run enters `run_initialized` and must emit `run_state_changed` before any judge step.\\\\n- **Continue:** each meaningful transition must emit `run_state_changed`; loops stop only on terminal states.\\\\n- **Public contract compatibility:** existing public contract is `terminal_status \\\\u2208 {passed|failed|escalated|aborted}` and `stop_reason \\\\u2208 {pass|budget_exhausted|escalated|aborted|policy_failed|evaluator_conflict|dependency_missing}` from `docs/skill-graphs/index.md`; implementation must normalize control states through event fields (not through custom status fields):\\\\n  - `run_completed` -> `terminal_status=passed`, `stop_reason=pass`\\\\n  - `run_failed` -> `terminal_status=failed`, `stop_reason=policy_failed`\\\\n  - `run_aborted` -> `terminal_status=aborted`, `stop_reason=aborted`\\\\n  - `run_rollforward_blocked` -> `terminal_status=failed`, `stop_reason=policy_failed`, blocker event `blocker_code=run_rollforward_blocked`\\\\n  - `run_rollback_required` -> `terminal_status=failed`, `stop_reason=dependency_missing`, blocker event `blocker_code=run_rollback_required`\\\\n- **Partial completion:** non-terminal checkpoints (`run_judgment_wait`, `run_adversarial_wait`, `run_operator_approval_required`) are explicit and must persist outputs for operator handoff.\\\\n- **Blocked state behavior:** duplicate run lock, stale resume token, CAS mismatch, or reviewer-policy rejection must transition to explicit blocked/rollback states, not implicit exits.\\\\n- **Kill-switch:** add a high-priority `--kill-switch-file` (or env-equivalent) checked before/after state transitions:\\\\n  - writes `run_state_changed` reason `kill_switch_activated`\\\\n  - emits terminal event `run_aborted`\\\\n  - releases run lock and persists a rollback recommendation record.\\\\n- **Rollback:** canonical lesson writes and promotion files must include lineage so rollback/replay can be reasoned from artifacts alone (version, predecessor id, expected-version origin, and operator).\\\\n- **Migration guard:** document this mapping as an explicit contract extension with explicit removal criteria in `docs/skill-graphs/schemas/gate-contract.schema.md` before Phase-4 enablement.\\\\n\\\\n#### Rollback / recovery invariants\\\\n- **Idempotency key + state lock** must gate duplicate processing attempts.\\\\n- **Expected-version CAS** is the normal path for safe re-promote; mismatch enters `run_rollforward_blocked` and emits explicit blocker event.\\\\n- **Recovery policy:** stale terminal output retries must be no-op, while non-terminal stale resumes must fail closed into `run_rollback_required`.\\\\n- **Operator controls:** kill-switch and allowlisted approve path are highest priority control planes and must preempt normal judge flow.\\\\n\\\\n### Research Insights\\\\n\\\\n**Best practices:**\\\\n- Treat the loop as a deterministic state machine with an explicit terminal-state enum and transitions validated by schema; every non-idempotent write should be keyed by run id.\\\\n- Apply two-level concurrency model: process-level mutex first, then artifact-level optimistic lock (CAS) before any canonical mutation.\\\\n- Separate \\\\u201ccontrol plane\\\\u201d events (approval, lock, kill, rollback) from \\\\u201ccandidate outcomes\\\\u201d events to simplify audit review.\\\\n\\\\n**Performance considerations:**\\\\n- Keep state writes append-only and periodic flushes frequent; avoid locking across long judge calls.\\\\n- Pre-create lock files with atomic rename to reduce races under concurrent starts.\\\\n\\\\n**Implementation details:**\\\\n- Consider explicit transition table in JSON Schema for allowed edges, with tests for illegal transitions.\\\\n- Add an invariant that blocked/rollback states must include a human-readable blocker plus machine-readable code.\\\\n\\\\n**Edge cases:**\\\\n- Concurrent starts with same run_id should be rejected before evaluation begins.\\\\n- Kill-switch asserted during active write should force immediate flush and avoid partial mutation; prefer two-phase commit style for canonical writes.\\\\n- Replay of a completed run should never re-open approval path.\\\\n\\\\n**References:**\\\\n- Python process locking and atomic file write patterns (temp-file rename semantics)\\\\n- **Objective:** Ensure every run is resumable, safely abortable, and auditable with deterministic completion semantics.\\\\n- **Constraints:** No silent failures, no hidden side effects, and operator control must always outrank normal loop progress.\\\\n- **Failure cost if wrong:** accidental duplicate promotions, incomplete audit trail, and unauthorized canonical graph mutation.\\\\n\\\\n#### Parity and control map (high priority paths)\\\\n| User action | Agent capability path | Current gap |\\\\n|---|---|---|\\\\n| Trigger loop run | `recursive_skill_loop.py` CLI options + run directory `run_state_changed` before any judge step.\\\\n- **Continue:** each meaningful transition must emit `run_state_changed`; loops stop only on terminal states.\\\\n- **Public contract compatibility:** existing public contract is `terminal_status \\\\u2208 {passed|failed|escalated|aborted}` and `stop_reason \\\\u2208 {pass|budget_exhausted|escalated|aborted|policy_failed|evaluator_conflict|dependency_missing}` from `docs/skill-graphs/index.md`; implementation must normalize control states through event fields (not through custom status fields):\\\\n  - `run_completed` -> `terminal_status=passed`, `stop_reason=pass`\\\\n  - `run_failed` -> `terminal_status=failed`, `stop_reason=policy_failed`\\\\n  - `run_aborted` -> `terminal_status=aborted`, `stop_reason=aborted`\\\\n  - `run_rollforward_blocked` -> `terminal_status=failed`, `stop_reason=policy_failed`, blocker event `blocker_code=run_rollforward_blocked`\\\\n  - `run_rollback_required` -> `terminal_status=failed`, `stop_reason=dependency_missing`, blocker event `blocker_code=run_rollback_required`\\\\n- **Partial completion:** non-terminal checkpoints (`run_judgment_wait`, `run_adversarial_wait`, `run_operator_approval_required`) are explicit and must persist outputs for operator handoff.\\\\n- **Blocked state behavior:** duplicate run lock, stale resume token, CAS mismatch, or reviewer-policy rejection must transition to explicit blocked/rollback states, not implicit exits.\\\\n- **Kill-switch:** add a high-priority `--kill-switch-file` (or env-equivalent) checked before/after state transitions:\\\\n  - writes `run_state_changed` reason `kill_switch_activated`\\\\n  - emits terminal event `run_aborted`\\\\n  - releases run lock and persists a rollback recommendation record.\\\\n- **Rollback:** canonical lesson writes and promotion files must include lineage so rollback/replay can be reasoned from artifacts alone (version, predecessor id, expected-version origin, and operator).\\\\n- **Migration guard:** document this mapping as an explicit contract extension with explicit removal criteria in `docs/skill-graphs/schemas/gate-contract.schema.md` before Phase-4 enablement.\\\\n\\\\n#### Rollback / recovery invariants\\\\n- **Idempotency key + state lock** must gate duplicate processing attempts.\\\\n- **Expected-version CAS** is the normal path for safe re-promote; mismatch enters `run_rollforward_blocked` and emits explicit blocker event.\\\\n- **Recovery policy:** stale terminal output retries must be no-op, while non-terminal stale resumes must fail closed into `run_rollback_required`.\\\\n- **Operator controls:** kill-switch and allowlisted approve path are highest priority control planes and must preempt normal judge flow.\\\\n\\\\n### Research Insights\\\\n\\\\n**Best practices:**\\\\n- Treat the loop as a deterministic state machine with an explicit terminal-state enum and transitions validated by schema; every non-idempotent write should be keyed by run id.\\\\n- Apply two-level concurrency model: process-level mutex first, then artifact-level optimistic lock (CAS) before any canonical mutation.\\\\n- Separate \\\\u201ccontrol plane\\\\u201d events (approval, lock, kill, rollback) from \\\\u201ccandidate outcomes\\\\u201d events to simplify audit review.\\\\n\\\\n**Performance considerations:**\\\\n- Keep state writes append-only and periodic flushes frequent; avoid locking across long judge calls.\\\\n- Pre-create lock files with atomic rename to reduce races under concurrent starts.\\\\n\\\\n**Implementation details:**\\\\n- Consider explicit transition table in JSON Schema for allowed edges, with tests for illegal transitions.\\\\n- Add an invariant that blocked/rollback states must include a human-readable blocker plus machine-readable code.\\\\n\\\\n**Edge cases:**\\\\n- Concurrent starts with same run_id should be rejected before evaluation begins.\\\\n- Kill-switch asserted during active write should force immediate flush and avoid partial mutation; prefer two-phase commit style for canonical writes.\\\\n- Replay of a completed run should never re-open approval path.\\\\n\\\\n**References:**\\\\n- Python process locking and atomic file write patterns (temp-file rename semantics)\\\\n- GitHub Actions artifact conventions and matrix-safe upload ordering\\\\n\\\\n## 1) Scope and boundaries\\\\n\\\\n### In scope\\\\n- I’d decide it by asking whether the proposed domain model changes the **repo’s shared conceptual control plane** or merely improves wording in one bounded area.\\n\\nA good rule:\\n\\n**Put it in core strategy when the model defines reusable concepts that other skills, docs, validators, sync flows, or agent workflows must understand consistently.**\\n\\nTreat it as **local terminology cleanup** when it only renames, clarifies, or tidies language inside one doc, one skill, one workflow, or one implementation area without changing shared behavior or cross-repo meaning.\\n\\n**Core Strategy Indicators**\\n\\nA proposed domain model belongs in the core strategy if several of these are true:\\n\\n1. It introduces or redefines canonical nouns  \\n   Examples: `skill`, `operator doc`, `runtime projection`, `canonical source`, `policy`, `sync`, `validation`, `proof`, `handle`, `agent workflow`.\\n\\n2. Multiple subsystems need the same meaning  \\n   If the term affects authoring, validation, discovery, syncing, runtime projection, docs, and CLI output, it is strategy-level.\\n\\n3. It changes ownership boundaries  \\n   If the model determines which paths are canonical versus generated, or which files agents should edit, it belongs in core strategy.\\n\\n4. It affects repo commands or robot-facing contracts  \\n   If `./bin/ask skills explain`, `skills prove`, `repo closeout`, or `--json --robot` output needs to reflect the model, it is core strategy.\\n\\n5. It affects validation or evidence rules  \\n   If the model changes what counts as valid, proven, synced, folded, stale, canonical, or agent-safe, it is not just terminology.\\n\\n6. It resolves a repeated conceptual confusion  \\n   If the same ambiguity appears across multiple docs, skills, or workflows, the model should be elevated so the repo has one shared language.\\n\\n7. It creates a stable abstraction future contributors must learn  \\n   If someone working elsewhere in the repo would need to understand the model to avoid making wrong edits, it belongs in core strategy.\\n\\n8. It needs to appear in `UBIQUITOUS_LANGUAGE.md`  \\n   This is probably the clearest signal from the repo instructions. If the concept belongs in the ubiquitous language, it is core strategy.\\n\\n**Local Cleanup Indicators**\\n\\nKeep it local if most of these are true:\\n\\n1. It only improves wording in one document or nearby set of docs.\\n\\n2. It does not alter any canonical/source/projection boundary.\\n\\n3. It does not affect CLI behavior, validation behavior, schemas, generated output, or agent-facing contracts.\\n\\n4. It is a synonym replacement rather than a new concept.\\n\\n5. The term is only meaningful in one workflow.\\n\\n6. Removing the term later would not break another doc’s meaning.\\n\\n7. It does not need to be taught to agents globally.\\n\\n8. It can be handled by editing the local doc and maybe adding a short inline definition.\\n\\n**Decision Test**\\n\\nI’d use this quick test:\\n\\n```text\\nIf an agent, validator, sync process, or contributor outside this local area\\nmust understand the model to make correct decisions, it belongs in core strategy.\\n\\nIf the model only makes this area easier to read without changing shared\\ndecision-making, it is local terminology cleanup.\\n```\\n\\n**Practical Classification**\\n\\nUse this matrix:\\n\\n| Question | Yes Means |\\n|---|---|\\n| Does it define canonical repo vocabulary? | Core strategy |\\n| Does it change what agents should edit? | Core strategy |\\n| Does it affect runtime projections or sync? | Core strategy |\\n| Does it affect validation/proof/closeout evidence? | Core strategy |\\n| Does it span multiple skills or docs? | Core strategy |\\n| Is it just renaming vague wording in one doc? | Local cleanup |\\n| Can it be understood fully from local context? | Local cleanup |\\n| Would `UBIQUITOUS_LANGUAGE.md` need updating? | Core strategy |\\n\\n**My Default Bias**\\n\\nI would bias toward **local terminology cleanup** unless the proposed model has real behavioral consequences or cross-cutting explanatory power.\\n\\nA lot of “domain model” proposals feel strategic because they introduce tidy nouns. The stronger test is whether those nouns change decisions:\\n\\n- What should be edited?\\n- What should be generated?\\n- What should be validated?\\n- What should agents trust?\\n- What should CLI commands expose?\\n- What should future docs reuse?\\n\\nIf the answers change, it is core strategy. If only prose gets clearer, keep it local.\\n\\n**Suggested Handling**\\n\\nFor a proposed model, I’d classify it like this:\\n\\n```text\\nClassification: Core strategy / Local terminology cleanup / Borderline\\n\\nReason:\\n- Scope:\\n- Affected paths:\\n- Affected commands:\\n- Affected validation or sync behavior:\\n- UBIQUITOUS_LANGUAGE.md impact:\\n- Recommendation:\\n```\\n\\nFor borderline cases, I’d usually do a two-step move:\\n\\n1. The most common failure mode in software development is misalignment. You think the dev knows what you want. Then you see what they've built - and you realize it didn't understand you at all.\\\\n\\\\nThis is just the same in the AI age. There is a communication gap between you and the agent. The fix for this is a **grilling session** - getting the agent to ask you detailed questions about what you're building.\\\\n\\\\n**The Fix** is to use:\\\\n\\\\n- [`/grill-me`](./skills/productivity/grill-me/SKILL.md) - for non-code uses\\\\n- [`/grill-with-docs`](./skills/engineering/grill-with-docs/SKILL.md) - same as [`/grill-me`](./skills/productivity/grill-me/SKILL.md), but adds more goodies (see below)\\\\n\\\\nThese are my most popular skills. They help you align with the agent before you get started, and think deeply about the change you're making. Use them _every_ time you want to make a change.\\\\n\\\\n### #2: The Agent Is Way Too Verbose\\\\n\\\\n> With a ubiquitous language, conversations among developers and expressions of the code are all derived from the same domain model.\\\\n>\\\\n> Eric Evans, [Domain-Driven-Design](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Domain-Driven-Design-Tackling-Complexity-Software/dp/0321125215)\\\\n\\\\n**The Problem**: At the start of a project, devs and the people they're building the software for (the domain experts) are usually speaking different languages.\\\\n\\\\nI felt the same tension with my agents. Agents are usually dropped into a project and asked to figure out the jargon as they go. So they use 20 words where 1 will do.\\\\n\\\\n**The Fix** for this is a shared language. It's a document that helps agents decode the jargon used in the project.\\\\n\\\\n<details>\\\\n<summary>\\\\nExample\\\\n</summary>\\\\n\\\\nHere's an example [`CONTEXT.md`](https://github.com/mattpocock/course-video-manager/blob/076a5a7a182db0fe1e62971dd7a68bcadf010f1c/CONTEXT.md), from my `course-video-manager` repo. Which one is easier to read?\\\\n\\\\n- **BEFORE**: \\\\\\\"There's a problem when a lesson inside a section of a course is made 'real' (i.e. given a spot in the file system)\\\\\\\"\\\\n- **AFTER**: \\\\\\\"There's a problem with the materialization cascade\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\nThis concision pays off session after session.\\\\n\\\\n</details>\\\\n\\\\nThis is built into [`/grill-with-docs`](./skills/engineering/grill-with-docs/SKILL.md). It's a grilling session, but that helps you build a shared language with the AI, and document hard-to-explain decisions in ADR's.\\\\n\\\\nIt's hard to explain how powerful this is. It might be the single coolest technique in this repo. Try it, and see.\\\\n\\\\n> [!TIP]\\\\n> A shared language has many other benefits than reducing verbosity:\\\\n>\\\\n> - **Variables, functions and files are named consistently**, using the shared language\\\\n> - As a result, the **codebase is easier to navigate** for the agent\\\\n> - The agent also **spends fewer tokens on thinking**, because it has access to a more concise language\\\\n\\\\n### #3: The Code Doesn't Work\\\\n\\\\n> \\\\\\\"Always take small, deliberate steps. The rate of feedback is your speed limit. Never take on a task that’s too big.\\\\\\\"\\\\n>\\\\n> David Thomas & Andrew Hunt, [The Pragmatic Programmer](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Pragmatic-Programmer-Anniversary-Journey-Mastery/dp/B0833F1T3V)\\\\n\\\\n**The Problem**: Let's say that you and the agent are aligned on what to build. What happens when the agent _still_ produces crap?\\\\n\\\\nIt's time to look at your feedback loops. Without feedback on how the code it produces actually runs, the agent will be flying blind.\\\\n\\\\n**The Fix**: You need the usual tranche of feedback loops: static types, browser access, and automated tests.\\\\n\\\\nFor automated tests, a red-green-refactor loop is critical. This is where the agent writes a failing test first, then fixes the test. This helps give the agent a consistent level of feedback that results in far better code.\\\\n\\\\nI've built a **[`/tdd`](./skills/engineering/tdd/SKILL.md) skill** you can slot into any project. It encourages red-green-refactor and gives the agent plenty of guidance on what makes good and bad tests.\\\\n\\\\nFor debugging, I've also built a **[`/diagnose`](./skills/engineering/diagnose/SKILL.md)** skill that wraps best debugging practices into a simple loop.\\\\n\\\\n### #4: We Built A Ball Of Mud\\\\n\\\\n> \\\\\\\"Invest in the design of the system _every day_.\\\\\\\"\\\\n>\\\\n> Kent Beck, [Extreme Programming Explained](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Extreme-Programming-Explained-Embrace-Change/dp/0321278658)\\\\n\\\\n> \\\\\\\"The best modules are deep. They allow a lot of functionality to be accessed through a simple interface.\\\\\\\"\\\\n>\\\\n> John Ousterhout, [A Philosophy Of Software Design](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Philosophy-Software-Design-2nd/dp/173210221X)\\\\n\\\\n**The Problem**: Most apps built with agents are complex and hard to change. Because agents can radically speed up coding, they also accelerate software entropy. Codebases get more complex at an unprecedented rate.\\\\n\\\\n**The Fix** for this is a radical new approach to AI-powered development: caring about the design of the code.\\\\n\\\\nThis is built in to every layer of these skills:\\\\n\\\\n- [`/to-prd`](./skills/engineering/to-prd/SKILL.md) quizzes you about which modules you're touching before creating a PRD\\\\n- [`/zoom-out`](./skills/engineering/zoom-out/SKILL.md) tells the agent to explain code in the context of the whole system\\\\n\\\\nAnd crucially, [`/improve-codebase-architecture`](./skills/engineering/improve-codebase-architecture/SKILL.md) helps you rescue a codebase that has become a ball of mud. I recommend running it on your codebase once every few days.\\\\n\\\\n### Summary\\\\n\\\\nSoftware engineering fundamentals matter more than ever.  \\\"name\\\": \\\"AGENT-BRIEF.md\\\",\\n  \\\"path\\\": \\\"skills/engineering/triage/AGENT-BRIEF.md\\\",\\n  \\\"sha\\\": \\\"2efecdfeb392246430a957de21d5062c2e5c98ba\\\",\\n  \\\"size\\\": 6243,\\n  \\\"url\\\": \\\"https://api.github.com/repos/mattpocock/skills/contents/skills/engineering/triage/AGENT-BRIEF.md?ref=main\\\",\\n  \\\"html_url\\\": \\\"https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/blob/main/skills/engineering/triage/AGENT-BRIEF.md\\\",\\n  \\\"git_url\\\": \\\"https://api.github.com/repos/mattpocock/skills/git/blobs/2efecdfeb392246430a957de21d5062c2e5c98ba\\\",\\n  \\\"download_url\\\": \\\"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mattpocock/skills/main/skills/engineering/triage/AGENT-BRIEF.md\\\",\\n  \\\"type\\\": \\\"file\\\",\\n  \\\"content\\\": \\\"# Writing Agent Briefs\\\\n\\\\nAn agent brief is a structured comment posted on a GitHub issue when it moves to `ready-for-agent`. It is the authoritative specification that an AFK agent will work from. The original issue body and discussion are context — the agent brief is the contract.\\\\n\\\\n## Principles\\\\n\\\\n### Durability over precision\\\\n\\\\nThe issue may sit in `ready-for-agent` for days or weeks. The codebase will change in the meantime. Write the brief so it stays useful even as files are renamed, moved, or refactored.\\\\n\\\\n- **Do** describe interfaces, types, and behavioral contracts\\\\n- **Do** name specific types, function signatures, or config shapes that the agent should look for or modify\\\\n- **Don't** reference file paths — they go stale\\\\n- **Don't** reference line numbers\\\\n- **Don't** assume the current implementation structure will remain the same\\\\n\\\\n### Behavioral, not procedural\\\\n\\\\nDescribe **what** the system should do, not **how** to implement it. The agent will explore the codebase fresh and make its own implementation decisions.\\\\n\\\\n- **Good:** \\\\\\\"The `SkillConfig` type should accept an optional `schedule` field of type `CronExpression`\\\\\\\"\\\\n- **Bad:** \\\\\\\"Open src/types/skill.ts and add a schedule field on line 42\\\\\\\"\\\\n- **Good:** \\\\\\\"When a user runs `/triage` with no arguments, they should see a summary of issues needing attention\\\\\\\"\\\\n- **Bad:** \\\\\\\"Add a switch statement in the main handler function\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\n### Complete acceptance criteria\\\\n\\\\nThe agent needs to know when it's done. Every agent brief must have concrete, testable acceptance criteria. Each criterion should be independently verifiable.\\\\n\\\\n- **Good:** \\\\\\\"Running `gh issue list --label needs-triage` returns issues that have been through initial classification\\\\\\\"\\\\n- **Bad:** \\\\\\\"Triage should work correctly\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\n### Explicit scope boundaries\\\\n\\\\nState what is out of scope. This prevents the agent from gold-plating or making assumptions about adjacent features.\\\\n\\\\n## Template\\\\n\\\\n```markdown\\\\n## Agent Brief\\\\n\\\\n**Category:** bug / enhancement\\\\n**Summary:** one-line description of what needs to happen\\\\n\\\\n**Current behavior:**\\\\nDescribe what happens now. For bugs, this is the broken behavior.\\\\nFor enhancements, this is the status quo the feature builds on.\\\\n\\\\n**Desired behavior:**\\\\nDescribe what should happen after the agent's work is complete.\\\\nBe specific about edge cases and error conditions.\\\\n\\\\n**Key interfaces:**\\\\n- `TypeName` — what needs to change and why\\\\n- `functionName()` return type — what it currently returns vs what it should return\\\\n- Config shape — any new configuration options needed\\\\n\\\\n**Acceptance criteria:**\\\\n- [ ] Specific, testable criterion 1\\\\n- [ ] Specific, testable criterion 2\\\\n- [ ] Specific, testable criterion 3\\\\n\\\\n**Out of scope:**\\\\n- Thing that should NOT be changed or addressed in this issue\\\\n- Adjacent feature that might seem related but is separate\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n## Examples\\\\n\\\\n### Good agent brief (bug)\\\\n\\\\n```markdown\\\\n## Agent Brief\\\\n\\\\n**Category:** bug\\\\n**Summary:** Skill description truncation drops mid-word, producing broken output\\\\n\\\\n**Current behavior:**\\\\nWhen a skill description exceeds 1024 characters, it is truncated at exactly\\\\n1024 characters regardless of word boundaries. This produces descriptions\\\\nthat end mid-word (e.g. \\\\\\\"Use when the user wants to confi\\\\\\\").\\\\n\\\\n**Desired behavior:**\\\\nTruncation should break at the last word boundary before 1024 characters\\\\nand append \\\\\\\"...\\\\\\\" to indicate truncation.\\\\n\\\\n**Key interfaces:**\\\\n- The `SkillMetadata` type's `description` field — no type change needed,\\\\n  but the validation/processing logic that populates it needs to respect\\\\n  word boundaries\\\\n- Any function that reads SKILL.md frontmatter and extracts the description\\\\n\\\\n**Acceptance criteria:**\\\\n- [ ] Descriptions under 1024 chars are unchanged\\\\n- [ ] Descriptions over 1024 chars are truncated at the last word boundary\\\\n      before 1024 chars\\\\n- [ ] Truncated descriptions end with \\\\\\\"...\\\\\\\"\\\\n- [ ] The total length including \\\\\\\"...\\\\\\\" does not exceed 1024 chars\\\\n\\\\n**Out of scope:**\\\\n- Changing the 1024 char limit itself\\\\n- Multi-line description support\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n### Good agent brief (enhancement)\\\\n\\\\n```markdown\\\\n## Agent Brief\\\\n\\\\n**Category:** enhancement\\\\n**Summary:** Add `.out-of-scope/` directory support for tracking rejected feature requests\\\\n\\\\n**Current behavior:**\\\\nWhen a feature request is rejected, the issue is closed with a `wontfix` label\\\\nand a comment. There is no persistent record of the decision or reasoning.\\\\nFuture similar requests require the maintainer to recall or search for the\\\\nprior discussion.\\\\n\\\\n**Desired behavior:**\\\\nRejected feature requests should be documented in `.out-of-scope/<concept>.md`\\\\nfiles that capture the decision, reasoning, and links to all issues that\\\\nrequested the feature. The most common failure mode in software development is misalignment. You think the dev knows what you want. agent brief is a structured comment posted on a GitHub issue when it moves to `ready-for-agent`. It is the authoritative specification that an AFK agent will work from. The original issue body and discussion are context — the agent brief is the contract.\\\\n\\\\n## Principles\\\\n\\\\n### Durability over precision\\\\n\\\\nThe issue may sit in `ready-for-agent` for days or weeks. The codebase will change in the meantime. Write the brief so it stays useful even as files are renamed, moved, or refactored.\\\\n\\\\n- **Do** describe interfaces, types, and behavioral contracts\\\\n- **Do** name specific types, function signatures, or config shapes that the agent should look for or modify\\\\n- **Don't** reference file paths — they go stale\\\\n- **Don't** reference line numbers\\\\n- **Don't** assume the current implementation structure will remain the same\\\\n\\\\n### Behavioral, not procedural\\\\n\\\\nDescribe **what** the system should do, not **how** to implement it. The agent will explore the codebase fresh and make its own implementation decisions.\\\\n\\\\n- **Good:** \\\\\\\"The `SkillConfig` type should accept an optional `schedule` field of type `CronExpression`\\\\\\\"\\\\n- **Bad:** \\\\\\\"Open src/types/skill.ts and add a schedule field on line 42\\\\\\\"\\\\n- **Good:** \\\\\\\"When a user runs `/triage` with no arguments, they should see a summary of issues needing attention\\\\\\\"\\\\n- **Bad:** \\\\\\\"Add a switch statement in the main handler function\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\n### Complete acceptance criteria\\\\n\\\\nThe agent needs to know when it's done. Every agent brief must have concrete, testable acceptance criteria. Each criterion should be independently verifiable.\\\\n\\\\n- **Good:** \\\\\\\"Running `gh issue list --label needs-triage` returns issues that have been through initial classification\\\\\\\"\\\\n- **Bad:** \\\\\\\"Triage should work correctly\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\n### Explicit scope boundaries\\\\n\\\\nState what is out of scope. This prevents the agent from gold-plating or making assumptions about adjacent features.\\\\n\\\\n## Template\\\\n\\\\n```markdown\\\\n## Agent Brief\\\\n\\\\n**Category:** bug / enhancement\\\\n**Summary:** one-line description of what needs to happen\\\\n\\\\n**Current behavior:**\\\\nDescribe what happens now. For bugs, this is the broken behavior.\\\\nFor enhancements, this is the status quo the feature builds on.\\\\n\\\\n**Desired behavior:**\\\\nDescribe what should happen after the agent's work is complete.\\\\nBe specific about edge cases and error conditions.\\\\n\\\\n**Key interfaces:**\\\\n- `TypeName` — what needs to change and why\\\\n- `functionName()` return type — what it currently returns vs what it should return\\\\n- Config shape — any new configuration options needed\\\\n\\\\n**Acceptance criteria:**\\\\n- [ ] Specific, testable criterion 1\\\\n- [ ] Specific, testable criterion 2\\\\n- [ ] Specific, testable criterion 3\\\\n\\\\n**Out of scope:**\\\\n- Thing that should NOT be changed or addressed in this issue\\\\n- Adjacent feature that might seem related but is separate\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n## Examples\\\\n\\\\n### Good agent brief (bug)\\\\n\\\\n```markdown\\\\n## Agent Brief\\\\n\\\\n**Category:** bug\\\\n**Summary:** Skill description truncation drops mid-word, producing broken output\\\\n\\\\n**Current behavior:**\\\\nWhen a skill description exceeds 1024 characters, it is truncated at exactly\\\\n1024 characters regardless of word boundaries. Based on the guidance you pasted, the claimed moat looks **partly real, but currently at risk of being mistaken for complexity**.\\n\\nThe strongest version of the moat is not “we have lots of docs, wrappers, policies, projections, and validation commands.” That is complexity. The real possible moat is:\\n\\n**Agent Skills Kit becomes the canonical control plane for repeatable agent behavior across authoring, validation, discovery, runtime projection, and synchronization.**\\n\\nThat is only a moat if the system makes agents and humans meaningfully better at producing reliable skills than they would be with ordinary markdown files, repo conventions, and CI checks.\\n\\n**What Looks Like Real Moat**\\nThe moat is credible where the system turns scattered agent instructions into enforceable operational leverage.\\n\\nThe strongest signals are:\\n\\n1. **Canonical source vs runtime projection**\\n   The phrase “edit canonical sources, not runtime projections” suggests the repo is trying to solve a real systems problem: skills need to exist in one authoritative form while being rendered or synced into agent-facing formats. If this is reliable, it is defensible because it creates a workflow others would have to reproduce, not just a pile of docs.\\n\\n2. **Robot-readable command surface**\\n   Commands like:\\n\\n   ```bash\\n   ./bin/ask skills explain <handle> --json --robot\\n   ./bin/ask skills prove <handle> --json --robot\\n   ./bin/ask repo closeout --changed --json --robot\\n   ```\\n\\n   are much more interesting than prose docs. They imply the system is designed for agents as first-class operators. That can become a moat if these commands expose stable contracts that let agents inspect, validate, improve, and close out work without bespoke repo knowledge.\\n\\n3. **Validation as part of the authoring loop**\\n   `skills prove`, `repo doctor`, and `repo closeout` imply quality gates around skill changes. If these checks catch real regressions in instruction quality, path ownership, projections, stale guidance, or discoverability, that is durable value.\\n\\n4. **Ubiquitous language**\\n   Requiring agents to read `UBIQUITOUS_LANGUAGE.md` before changing skills is a good sign. Moats often come from shared mental models, especially in systems where humans and agents both need to coordinate. If the repo has a precise vocabulary for “skill,” “runtime projection,” “canonical source,” “operator docs,” “sync policy,” etc., that reduces coordination cost.\\n\\n5. **Path ownership boundaries**\\n   The explicit distinction between canonical sources and generated/runtime surfaces is the kind of boring governance that becomes valuable when a system scales. Most agent instruction repos collapse under ambiguous ownership. If this repo prevents that, it has real infrastructure value.\\n\\n**What Looks Like Complexity Masquerading As Moat**\\nThe dangerous version is that the project has built a lot of process around something that might ultimately be simple: “a directory of markdown instructions with a validator.”\\n\\nThe warning signs:\\n\\n1. **Too many control documents**\\n   The pasted guide points to at least seven separate docs:\\n\\n   ```text\\n   02-tooling-policy.md\\n   04-validation.md\\n   05-contradictions-and-cleanup.md\\n   13-workflow-and-safety-guidance.md\\n   14-path-ownership-boundaries.md\\n   16-agent-operating-contract.md\\n   17-skill-management.md\\n   18-browser-and-local-preview.md\\n   ```\\n\\n   That may be necessary, but it is also a smell. If agents need to absorb a large policy graph before making safe changes, the system may be exporting complexity to its operators instead of encapsulating it.\\n\\n2. **The root wrapper may hide too much**\\n   “Use `./bin/ask` for repo operations” can be excellent if it gives agents a narrow, stable control surface. It can also become a black box that prevents contributors from understanding what is actually being validated.\\n\\n   The moat depends on whether `./bin/ask` is a clean product interface or just a convenience wrapper around fragile internal conventions.\\n\\n3. **Skill improvement may be performative**\\n   This command is especially important:\\n\\n   ```bash\\n   ./bin/ask skills improve \\\"<goal>\\\" --json --robot\\n   ```\\n\\n   If it produces actionable diffs, validates them, and improves measurable behavior, that is powerful. If it mostly rewrites prose, shuffles instruction wording, or adds meta-guidance without evaluation, then the “self-improving skills” claim is more theater than moat.\\n\\n4. **Policy synchronization can become bureaucracy**\\n   Syncing policy, runtime projections, and agent-facing docs sounds useful, but only if drift is common and expensive. If drift is rare, or if users do not actually rely on the projections, then the system is paying a permanent complexity tax for an occasional problem.\\n\\n5. **The repo may be overfitted to Codex**\\n   The docs call this the canonical control plane for “Codex skills, operator docs, and agent workflows.” That is a valid niche, but the broader moat depends on whether the concepts generalize across agents, environments, and teams. If the abstractions only work inside one user’s local workflow, the moat is local productivity, not market defensibility.\\n\\n**The Core Test**\\nThe moat is real if the system creates one or more compounding advantages:\\n\\n1. **Better skills get easier to produce over time**\\n   Each new skill should benefit from prior validation rules, templates, vocabulary, examples, and closeout automation.\\n\\n2. **Agent reliability improves measurably**\\n   The system should reduce wrong-file edits, stale instruction use, invalid runtime projections, broken skill metadata, and incomplete validation.\\n\\n3. **The command surface becomes an API**\\n   `./bin/ask` should feel like a stable agent-native API, not a bag of scripts. If other agents can operate the repo through `--json --robot` without reading large amounts of prose, that is moat.\\n\\n4. **The source/projection model prevents real damage**\\n   If runtime projection drift or accidental projection edits have historically caused bugs, and this repo prevents them, that is genuine operational moat.\\n\\n5. **The system has memory**\\n   Not necessarily LLM memory, but institutional memory: cleanup docs, contradiction tracking, validation evidence, explain/prove commands, and repeatable closeout. That can be quite defensible.\\n\\nThe moat is fake if the system mainly creates:\\n\\n1. More documents to read.\\n2. More command wrappers to remember.\\n3. More distinction-making without measurable quality gains.\\n4. More agent hesitation before edits.\\n5. More bespoke concepts than the value of the skills themselves justifies.\\n\\n**My Verdict**\\nI would call the moat **conditionally real**.\\n\\nThe promising part is the combination of:\\n\\n```text\\ncanonical source of truth\\nruntime projections\\nagent-readable command contracts\\nvalidation/proof commands\\npath ownership boundaries\\nrepo closeout evidence\\n```\\n\\nThat is a coherent control-plane thesis. It is not just “we wrote better prompts.” It is closer to “we built a governed operating system for agent skills.”\\n\\nBut the moat is fragile because the same ingredients can easily decay into ceremony. The real moat is **not the complexity itself**. The real moat is whether the complexity is hidden behind simple, reliable agent-native operations.\\n\\nIn sharper terms:\\n\\n**If `./bin/ask` lets an agent safely understand, modify, validate, and close out skill work with less context than a human would need, the moat is real.**\\n\\n**If agents still need to read a web of policy docs and manually reason about ownership, sync state, validation order, and stale guidance, then the system is mostly complexity with a good story around it.**\\n\\n**Pressure-Test Questions**\\nI’d use these to separate moat from mess:\\n\\n1. Can a new agent safely modify a skill after reading only `AGENTS.md`, `UBIQUITOUS_LANGUAGE.md`, and the output of `./bin/ask skills explain <handle> --json --robot`?\\n\\n2. Does `./bin/ask skills prove <handle> --json --robot` catch failures that a normal markdown linter would miss?\\n\\n3. Are runtime projections generated deterministically from canonical sources, with drift detectable by tooling?\\n\\n4. How often do contributors accidentally edit projections, violate ownership boundaries, or leave stale guidance, and how much has this system reduced that?\\n\\n5. Does `skills improve` produce changes that survive adversarial review, or does it mostly add polish?\\n\\n6. Is the system easier to use at 100 skills than at 10 skills?\\n\\n7. Can another repo adopt the same model without copying a large amount of local lore?\\n\\n8. Are the concepts independently valuable, or do they only make sense because the current repo has already accumulated complexity?\\n\\n9. Do the validation commands produce evidence good enough for review, CI, or release gating?\\n\\n10. Can the repo explain why a skill exists, where it projects, how it is validated, and what depends on it without a human spelunking the tree?\\n\\n**Best Framing**\\nThe claimed moat should probably not be framed as:\\n\\n> “We have a sophisticated skill management system.”\\n\\nThat invites the complexity critique.\\n\\nIt should be framed as:\\n\\n> “We turn agent instructions into governed, testable, discoverable, projection-safe assets that agents can operate through stable robot-readable contracts.”\\n\\nThat is a much stronger claim.
